tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

I should look at the manifest types, the remote install/tag resolution code, and where the post-run version check hook currently lives to figure out where to wire this in. My plan is to mirror the existing version-check pattern but scoped to plugins: a separate cache file with the same 24-hour interval and silent-failure behavior, triggered only for the specific plugin that was just invoked rather than scanning every installed plugin, since checking on use keeps it cheap and matches how the CLI checks itself.

I should read types.go, the root.go hook, and autoupdate.go to understand tag resolution and gating, and also check whether the cli repo has its own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md with repo-specific conventions I should follow before touching plugin.go's dispatch logic.

input.title: CLI: update notice for outdated plugins, mirroring the CLI's own version check
input.description:
## Problem

The CLI notifies the user when the `entire` binary is outdated: a version check runs after commands, caches its result for 24 hours, and prints "Update available! x -> y" to stderr (`versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`). Installed plugins have no equivalent. A user on an old plugin version sees nothing until they manually run `entire plugin upgrade`.

## Approach

Reuse the proven mechanisms; no new design.

- **Trigger**: after a successful plugin run, next to the existing CLI version notice in the plugin dispatch path (`plugin.go`). Check only the plugin that ran.
- **Latest version**: `listRemoteSemverTags` on the manifest's repo URL — the same resolution `entire plugin upgrade` uses (stable semver tags only, prereleases excluded).
- **Cadence**: 24-hour per-plugin cache in the global config dir, beside `version_check.json`. The cache updates even when the fetch fails, so a network problem does not retry on every invocation. Silent on all errors. All mirrored from `versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`.
- **Notice** (stderr, mirrors the CLI banner's non-interactive form):

  ```
  Plugin update available! brain 0.2.0 -> 0.3.0
  To update, run:
    entire plugin upgrade brain
  ```

- **Skipped**: plugins without an install manifest (local-dev symlinks, binaries dropped on PATH) and pinned installs — the same installs `plugin upgrade` skips.

## Non-goals

- Interactive auto-upgrade prompt (parity with `maybeAutoUpdate`). Plugin runs are mostly agent-driven and non-interactive; the printed command is the useful part. Can follow up if wanted.
- Checking plugins other than the one being run.
- New kill-switch env vars.

+	// origins × per-origin-timeout equals the loop's own worst case, so it
+	// can never bind. Keeping it at the historical 2s means adding a second

content.content:
21:   The set is deliberately narrow, and membership is not a reward for being official — `run` and `upgrade` are both index-listed and both absent from it. The offer is a prompt defaulting to Yes that ends in a downloaded binary linked onto `$PATH`, so it belongs only to former built-ins and to commands Entire's docs or generated agent guides tell people to run as `entire <name>` — names a user types because we told them the command exists. `graph` is what Brain's agent guide sends agents to (`entire graph search`); `brain` is documented as `entire brain`; `investigate` was a built-in until it moved to the entire-investigate plugin, and without the offer an established command would answer with Cobra's "unknown command".
40:`entire plugin install/list/remove/upgrade` manage the contents of this directory. Authors who prefer the raw "drop a binary on `$PATH`" model don't need to use it.
44:`entire plugin install`, `entire plugin upgrade`, dependency installs, and the on-demand `entire graph` install report their stages — index lookup, release metadata, download and checksum verification, placement — on **stderr**, so stdout carries only the result and stays pipeable. A styled terminal gets a spinner; a non-terminal writer and accessibility mode get one plain line per stage as it starts. Progress stops before any confirmation or result is printed, including on failure. Asset-name probing shares one download status per release rather than one per candidate.
62:1. **Version resolution** uses `git ls-remote --tags` — identical on GitHub, GitLab, Gitea/Forgejo, and self-hosted servers; inherits the user's git auth and proxy config. The highest **stable** semver tag wins; `--pin <tag>` installs exactly that tag and marks the manifest pinned (skipped by `upgrade`).
64:   Prereleases are excluded from resolution. semver ranks `v2.0.0-rc1` above stable `v1.9.0`, so listing them would move every user onto a release candidate on the next `plugin upgrade --all` the moment an author pushed one. `--pin` is the opt-in, since it bypasses listing entirely. Every git subprocess also carries a two-minute deadline — the root context is cancellable but has no timeout, so an unreachable host would otherwise hang the command with no output, which matters most during dependency planning against author-controlled URLs.
66:3. **Asset download** is the one forge-specific step, contained in a small URL-convention table: GitHub/Gitea-style `<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<asset>`, GitLab-style `<repo>/-/releases/<tag>/downloads/<asset>`, unknown hosts default to GitHub-style. Authors on other hosts declare a `download_url` template in `entire-plugin.yml` (placeholders: `{name}` `{tag}` `{version}` `{os}` `{arch}` `{asset}`).
67:4. **Asset selection** goes through the release's `checksums.txt`: the manifest lists what was actually published, and the download is verified against it. Candidate names follow goreleaser conventions (`entire-<name>_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz` and friends, with `x86_64`/`aarch64` aliases and a `darwin_all` universal-binary fallback (`all` occupies the *arch* slot, which is where goreleaser puts it)). A pushed tag with no published assets falls back to the next-highest tag with a warning.
76:Selection among candidates is deterministic: shallowest path first, then lexicographic. Matching is by basename, so an archive can legitimately hold several — the binary at the root, the same name nested under a versioned directory (goreleaser's `wrap_in_directory`), and unrelated files such as `completions/entire-<name>`. Taking whichever came first made the installed binary depend on the order the author's tar was built in. For tar this costs a second pass, since the stream cannot seek backwards.

**A miss forces one index refresh before it is believed.** The catalog clone refreshes on a 24-hour TTL, so a plugin added today is invisible to every cached copy for up to a day — and the "not listed in the plugin index" error then blames the catalog for being out of date when the local copy is the stale one. That is precisely the window after a new plugin is published, which is when someone is most likely to try installing it. The retry runs only on a path already about to fail and exit non-zero, only for the names in this set, and never on the hit path; offline it cannot make things worse, because `SyncPluginIndex` falls back to the stale copy with a logged warning rather than failing, so the worst case is the same miss and the same message.

   A `graph` that is already in the [managed install directory](#managed-install-directory) but unreachable through `$PATH` — a managed dir that could not be prepended at startup — is **executed**, not offered for installation. Installing over it cannot work: an existing install needs `--force`, which the on-demand path deliberately does not pass, so prompting would spend the user's Yes and several network round-trips on a guaranteed "already installed; use --force to replace".

   A managed entry that exists but **cannot be run** — a local-dev symlink whose target moved, an empty file, or a directory in its place — is reported with its path and the same repair `entire plugin doctor` gives: for a release install, a reinstall from the recorded source (`entire plugin install <url> --force`, keeping `--pin` and `--allow-unverified`); for a manifest-less local-dev entry, rebuild the target or `entire plugin remove <name>`. It is neither executed (a `fork/exec` ENOENT names a path the user never chose) nor reinstalled over: replacing a developer's deliberate symlink with a released binary is their call.

### Managed install directory

Users can drop binaries anywhere on `$PATH`, but a per-user managed directory is also automatically discovered:

- **Default:** `$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire/plugins/bin` (Linux/macOS) or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\entire\plugins\bin` (Windows).
- **Override:** `$ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR/bin`.

The CLI prepends this directory to `$PATH` at startup via `cli.PrependPluginBinDirToPATH()` so the existing `exec.LookPath` resolution finds managed installs without any special-casing. This is purely additive — the kubectl-style `$PATH` model is unchanged.

`entire plugin install/list/remove/upgrade` manage the contents of this directory. Authors who prefer the raw "drop a binary on `$PATH`" model don't need to use it.

### Install progress and confirmations

`entire plugin install`, `entire plugin upgrade`, dependency installs, and the on-demand `entire graph` install report their stages — index lookup, release metadata, download and checksum verification, placement — on **stderr**, so stdout carries only the result and stays pipeable. A styled terminal gets a spinner; a non-terminal writer and accessibility mode get one plain line per stage as it starts. Progress stops before any confirmation or result is printed, including on failure. Asset-name probing shares one download status per release rather than one per candidate.

- **Default:** `$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire/plugins/bin` (Linux/macOS) or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\entire\plugins\bin` (Windows).
- **Override:** `$ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR/bin`.

The CLI prepends this directory to `$PATH` at startup via `cli.PrependPluginBinDirToPATH()` so the existing `exec.LookPath` resolution finds managed installs without any special-casing. This is purely additive — the kubectl-style `$PATH` model is unchanged.

`entire plugin install/list/remove/upgrade` manage the contents of this directory. Authors who prefer the raw "drop a binary on `$PATH`" model don't need to use it.

### Install progress and confirmations

`entire plugin install`, `entire plugin upgrade`, dependency installs, and the on-demand `entire graph` install report their stages — index lookup, release metadata, download and checksum verification, placement — on **stderr**, so stdout carries only the result and stays pipeable. A styled terminal gets a spinner; a non-terminal writer and accessibility mode get one plain line per stage as it starts. Progress stops before any confirmation or result is printed, including on failure. Asset-name probing shares one download status per release rather than one per candidate.

### Install progress and confirmations

`entire plugin install`, `entire plugin upgrade`, dependency installs, and the on-demand `entire graph` install report their stages — index lookup, release metadata, download and checksum verification, placement — on **stderr**, so stdout carries only the result and stays pipeable. A styled terminal gets a spinner; a non-terminal writer and accessibility mode get one plain line per stage as it starts. Progress stops before any confirmation or result is printed, including on failure. Asset-name probing shares one download status per release rather than one per candidate.

Progress travels on the context (`withPluginProgress`), so a caller that has not opted in prints nothing — a library caller never writes to the process's terminal on its own.

Confirmations read from the **controlling terminal**, never stdin, so a plugin's piped input survives being prompted about. They render to the writer the caller supplies, except when that writer is not itself a terminal (`entire graph 2>log`): then the prompt renders on the terminal the answer is read from, because a prompt nobody can see still blocks on a keypress — and with Yes as the default, an unwitting Enter would authorize the install. An input that reaches EOF never becomes a Yes, but the two modes get there differently: accessibility mode declines outright — huh's scanner would otherwise read EOF as the field's default, which is Yes here — while the default full-screen prompt keeps waiting until the context is cancelled. Both fail closed; only one of them answers. Cancellation stops the prompt either way, and still terminates by signal.

### Update notice

After a successful dispatched run, the CLI checks whether the plugin that ran has a newer stable tag and prints a notice on stderr (`Plugin update available! <name> x -> y`, followed by the `entire plugin upgrade <name>` command). It mirrors the CLI's own post-run version check: one remote lookup per plugin per 24 hours, the cache (`plugin_version_check.json`, beside `version_check.json` in the global config dir) stamped even when the lookup fails so a dead remote is not retried on every invocation, and silence on every error. The latest version comes from the same stable-tag resolution `plugin upgrade` uses, but bounded to the version check's 2-second budget rather than the 2-minute git deadline, because it runs synchronously after every plugin exit. # Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [0.12.2] - 2026-10-26

### Added

- `entire enable` ends by listing the Entire configuration that still needs committing (`.entire/settings.json`, `.entire/.gitignore`, and each agent's hook config and skill files), since other worktrees and clones only get the setup once it is committed. In an interactive terminal it offers to commit exactly those files and leaves anything else you had staged alone. The default answer is Yes when setup created a file and No when every listed file was already tracked. With `--yes`, without a TTY, or during a merge or rebase it only prints the list, and `entire agent add` only lists. Nothing is pushed ([#2893](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2893))
- `transcript.jsonl` assistant lines carry per-call usage for Claude Code, Codex and Pi: the call's `model`, fresh `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens` (with the 5m/1h split when the agent reports it) and `reasoning_tokens`. Codex writes one assistant line per model call. Older lines stay readable and the format version is still 1 ([#2834](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2834), [#2889](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2889), [#2858](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2858), [#2859](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2859), [#2862](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2862))
- With `redaction.externalize_images` on, Pi images move to `assets/` like Claude Code and Codex images. Pi user turns that hold only an image are no longer dropped from `transcript.jsonl` ([#2891](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2891))

### Changed

- The first-turn context Entire injects into agent sessions now goes out in every session, not only where trails are enabled. It points agents at `entire agent-help`; the trail guidance is added only when trails are enabled, on a later turn if that is learned after the session starts. Agents may create checkpoints manually when the user asks, and are told to ask before running setup or destructive commands ([#2887](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2887))
- `entire trail comment` write commands (`add`, `reply`, `edit`, `delete`, `resolve`, `unresolve`) refuse when run from an agent session and point at `entire trail finding` instead, since trail comments are for people. `list` and `show` still work for agents. agent-help and the injected context say the same ([#2890](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2890))
- `entire trail` is listed in `entire help` under a new "Trails:" group ([#2896](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2896))

### Fixed

- A commit no longer gets an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer for an idle session whose new work is only in its live transcript without that checkpoint being written. Such sessions are now condensed at commit, and in stacked worktrees that touch the same files only the session's own worktree picks up its work ([#2892](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2892))

### Housekeeping

- The `transcript` library's Pi JSONL parser moved to an internal package, and the unused Claude Code and Codex native-reader API was removed ([#2832](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/2832))

## [0.12.1] - 2026-10-24

cd ~/code/entire/cli && git push origin evisdren/ent-3598-plugin-update-notice && gh pr create --base main --title "plugin: notify when the plugin that just ran has a newer release" --body "## Why

The CLI tells the user when the \`entire\` binary is outdated (24h-cached post-run check, stderr banner), but installed plugins have no equivalent: a user on an old plugin version sees nothing until they manually run \`entire plugin upgrade\`.

Linear: ENT-3598 · Trail: #2601

## What

After a successful plugin run, the dispatcher checks whether that plugin has a newer stable tag and prints on stderr:

\`\`\`
Plugin update available! brain 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0
To update, run:
  entire plugin upgrade brain
\`\`\`

No new machinery — it mirrors \`versioncheck.CheckAndNotify\` step for step:

- 24h per-plugin cache (\`plugin_version_check.json\`, beside \`version_check.json\`), stamped even when the lookup fails so a dead remote is not retried every invocation; silent on all errors; same atomic write-then-rename.
- Latest version from \`listRemoteSemverTags\` — the exact resolution \`plugin upgrade\` uses (stable tags only), so the notice can never name a version upgrade would not install.
- Bounded to the version check's 2s budget, not the 2-minute plugin git deadline, since it runs synchronously after every plugin exit.
- Pinned and manifest-less installs (local-dev symlinks, PATH drops) are skipped — the same installs \`upgrade\` skips.
- Wired beside the existing CLI version notice in \`plugin.go\`, same test-seam pattern.

Documented in \`docs/architecture/external-commands.md\` (\"Update notice\").

## Validation

- New tests: notice when outdated, silence when up to date, 24h cache suppresses re-checks, failed fetch is silent and stamps the cache, pinned skip, manifest-less skip.
- \`mise run fmt\`, \`mise run lint\`, unit + integration suites all pass locally.
- The e2e canary lane could not run on this machine (missing \`gotestsum\`/\`tmux\`); relying on CI for it.

content.text:
{"id":"ENT-3598","uuid":"20b00a2f-9e11-4b23-9498-1dc31203bcda","title":"CLI: update notice for outdated plugins, mirroring the CLI's own version check","description":"## Problem

The CLI notifies the user when the `entire` binary is outdated: a version check runs after commands, caches its result for 24 hours, and prints "Update available! x -> y" to stderr (`versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`). Installed plugins have no equivalent. A user on an old plugin version sees nothing until they manually run `entire plugin upgrade`.

## Approach

Reuse the proven mechanisms; no new design.

* **Trigger**: after a successful plugin run, next to the existing CLI version notice in the plugin dispatch path (`plugin.go`). Check only the plugin that ran.
* **Latest version**: `listRemoteSemverTags` on the manifest's repo URL — the same resolution `entire plugin upgrade` uses (stable semver tags only, prereleases excluded).
* **Cadence**: 24-hour per-plugin cache in the global config dir, beside `version_check.json`. The cache updates even when the fetch fails, so a network problem does not retry on every invocation. Silent on all errors. All mirrored from `versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`.
* **Notice** (stderr, mirrors the CLI banner's non-interactive form):

  ```
  Plugin update available! brain 0.2.0 -> 0.3.0
  To update, run:
    entire plugin upgrade brain
  ```
* **Skipped**: plugins without an install manifest (local-dev symlinks, binaries dropped on PATH) and pinned installs — the same installs `plugin upgrade` skips.

## Non-goals

* Interactive auto-upgrade prompt (parity with `maybeAutoUpdate`). Plugin runs are mostly agent-driven and non-interactive; the printed command is the useful part. Can follow up if wanted.
* Checking plugins other than the one being run.

content.text:
# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

new file mode 100644
index 0000000000..a46e336d14
--- /dev/null
+++ b/cmd/entire/cli/plugin_versioncheck.go
@@ -0,0 +1,159 @@
+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"fmt"
+	"io"
+	"strings"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/jsonutil"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/logging"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/osroot"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/internal/entireclient/userdirs"
+	"golang.org/x/mod/semver"
+)
+
+// This file mirrors versioncheck.CheckAndNotify for installed plugins: a
+// post-run notice, a 24h cache stamped even when the lookup fails, and
+// silence on every error path. The latest version comes from the same tag
+// resolution `entire plugin upgrade` uses, so the notice can never name a
+// version the upgrade would not install.
+
+const (
+	// pluginCheckInterval mirrors versioncheck's checkInterval.
+	pluginCheckInterval = 24 * time.Hour
+
+	// pluginCheckTimeout mirrors versioncheck's httpTimeout: the check runs
+	// synchronously after the plugin has exited, so the remote tag listing
+	// gets the same 2s budget the CLI's own post-run check lives within,
+	// not the much larger interactive-install git timeout.
+	pluginCheckTimeout = 2 * time.Second
+
+	// pluginCacheFileName sits beside versioncheck's version_check.json in
+	// the global config directory.
+	pluginCacheFileName = "plugin_version_check.json"
+)
+
+// pluginVersionCache is the plugin analog of versioncheck.VersionCache,
+// keyed by plugin name. No SkippedVersion: there is no interactive prompt,
+// so there is no "skip this version" choice to remember.
+type pluginVersionCache struct {
+	Plugins map[string]pluginVersionCheckState `json:"plugins"`
+}
+
+type pluginVersionCheckState struct {
+	LastCheckTime time.Time `json:"last_check_time"`
+}
+
+// listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck is a test seam over the tag resolution
+// `entire plugin upgrade` uses.
+var listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = listRemoteSemverTags
+
+// checkPluginUpdateAndNotify prints an update notice for pluginName when a
+// newer stable tag than the installed one exists. Silent on all errors to
+// avoid interrupting plugin runs, mirroring versioncheck.CheckAndNotify.
+//
+// Plugins without an install manifest (local-dev symlinks, binaries dropped
+// on PATH) and pinned installs are skipped — the same installs
+// `entire plugin upgrade` skips.
+func checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, pluginName string) {
+	m, err := LoadPluginManifest(pluginName)
+	if err != nil || m == nil {
+		return
+	}
+	if m.Pinned {
+		return
+	}
+
+	cache := loadPluginVersionCache()
+	if time.Since(cache.Plugins[pluginName].LastCheckTime) < pluginCheckInterval {
+		return
+	}
+
+	tagCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, pluginCheckTimeout)
+	tags, err := listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck(tagCtx, m.RepoURL)
+	cancel()
+
+	// Always stamp the cache so a failing remote is not retried on every
+	// invocation.
+	cache.Plugins[pluginName] = pluginVersionCheckState{LastCheckTime: time.Now()}
+	if saveErr := savePluginVersionCache(cache); saveErr != nil {
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "plugin version check: failed to save cache",
+			"plugin", pluginName, "error", saveErr.Error())
+	}
+
+	if err != nil {
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "plugin version check: failed to list tags",
+			"plugin", pluginName, "error", err.Error())
+		return
+	}
+	if len(tags) == 0 {
+		return
+	}
+
+	// Same comparison UpgradeInstalledPlugin makes before reinstalling.
+	latest := tags[0]
+	if semver.Compare(canonicalSemver(latest), canonicalSemver(m.Tag)) <= 0 {
+		return
+	}
+
+	fmt.Fprintf(w, "\nPlugin update available! %s %s -> %s\nTo update, run:\n  entire plugin upgrade %s\n",
+		pluginName, strings.TrimPrefix(m.Tag, "v"), strings.TrimPrefix(latest, "v"), pluginName)
+}
+
+// loadPluginVersionCache returns the cached per-plugin check times, or an
+// empty cache when the file is missing or unreadable — mirroring how
+// versioncheck treats its cache file.
+func loadPluginVersionCache() *pluginVersionCache {
+	empty := &pluginVersionCache{Plugins: map[string]pluginVersionCheckState{}}
+	root, err := userdirs.ConfigRootForRead()
+	if err != nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	data, err := osroot.ReadFileNoFollow(root, pluginCacheFileName)
+	if err != nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	var cache pluginVersionCache
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &cache); err != nil || cache.Plugins == nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	return &cache
+}
+
+// savePluginVersionCache writes the cache with the same atomic
+// write-then-rename versioncheck's saveCache uses. Going through
+// userdirs.ConfigRoot also creates the config directory with private
+// permissions when this runs before first login.
+func savePluginVersionCache(cache *pluginVersionCache) error {
+	data, err := json.MarshalIndent(cache, "", "  ")
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("marshaling cache: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	root, err := userdirs.ConfigRoot()
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("opening config directory: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	tmpFile, tmpName, err := jsonutil.CreateTempIn(root, pluginCacheFileName)
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("creating temp file: %w", err)
+	}
+	defer func() { _ = root.Remove(tmpName) }() //nolint:errcheck // best-effort; a successful rename already consumed it
+
+	if _, err := tmpFile.Write(data); err != nil {
+		_ = tmpFile.Close() // cleanup on error path
+		return fmt.Errorf("writing cache: %w", err)
+	}
+	if err := tmpFile.Close(); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("closing temp file: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	if err := root.Rename(tmpName, pluginCacheFileName); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("renaming cache file: %w", err)
+	}
+	return nil
+}

+package cli
+

+
+// setupPluginUpdateCheck isolates the managed plugin dir and the global
+// config dir (where the check's cache lives), installs a manifest for
+// "brain" at v0.1.0, and stubs the remote tag listing.
+func setupPluginUpdateCheck(t *testing.T, manifest *PluginManifest, tags []string, tagsErr error) *int {
+	t.Helper()
+	withPluginDir(t)
+	t.Setenv(userdirs.EnvConfigDir, t.TempDir())
+	if manifest != nil {
+		if err := SavePluginManifest(manifest); err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("SavePluginManifest: %v", err)
+		}
+	}
+	calls := 0
+	orig := listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck
+	listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = func(context.Context, string) ([]string, error) {
+		calls++
+		return tags, tagsErr
+	}
+	t.Cleanup(func() { listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = orig })
+	return &calls
+}
+
+func brainManifest() *PluginManifest {
+	return &PluginManifest{Name: "brain", RepoURL: "https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain", Tag: "v0.1.0"}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_NotifiesWhenOutdated(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"v0.2.0", "v0.1.0"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1", *calls)
+	}
+	got := out.String()
+	for _, want := range []string{"Plugin update available! brain 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0", "entire plugin upgrade brain"} {
+		if !strings.Contains(got, want) {
+			t.Errorf("notice %q missing %q", got, want)
+		}
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SilentWhenUpToDate(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	// "0.1.0" vs installed "v0.1.0": equal under semver, so no notice —
+	// same spelling tolerance UpgradeInstalledPlugin has.
+	setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"0.1.0"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output, got %q", out.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_CacheSuppressesRecheck(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"v0.2.0"}, nil)
+
+	var first, second strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &first, "brain")
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &second, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1 (second call must hit the 24h cache)", *calls)
+	}
+	if second.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output on cached call, got %q", second.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_FetchFailureIsSilentAndStampsCache(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), nil, errors.New("network down"))
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output, got %q", out.String())
+	}
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1 (a failed check must not retry within 24h)", *calls)
+	}
+	state := loadPluginVersionCache().Plugins["brain"]
+	if time.Since(state.LastCheckTime) > time.Minute {
+		t.Fatalf("cache not stamped after failed fetch: %v", state.LastCheckTime)
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SkipsPinned(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	m := brainManifest()
+	m.Pinned = true
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, m, []string{"v9.9.9"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 0 || out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("pinned plugin checked remote (%d calls) or printed %q", *calls, out.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SkipsWithoutManifest(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, nil, []string{"v9.9.9"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 0 || out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("manifest-less plugin checked remote (%d calls) or printed %q", *calls, out.String())

+}

+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"encoding/json"
+	"fmt"
+	"io"
+	"strings"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/jsonutil"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/logging"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/osroot"
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/internal/entireclient/userdirs"
+	"golang.org/x/mod/semver"
+)
+
+// This file mirrors versioncheck.CheckAndNotify for installed plugins: a
+// post-run notice, a 24h cache stamped even when the lookup fails, and
+// silence on every error path. The latest version comes from the same tag
+// resolution `entire plugin upgrade` uses, so the notice can never name a
+// version the upgrade would not install.
+
+const (
+	// pluginCheckInterval mirrors versioncheck's checkInterval.
+	pluginCheckInterval = 24 * time.Hour
+
+	// pluginCheckTimeout mirrors versioncheck's httpTimeout: the check runs
+	// synchronously after the plugin has exited, so the remote tag listing
+	// gets the same 2s budget the CLI's own post-run check lives within,
+	// not the much larger interactive-install git timeout.
+	pluginCheckTimeout = 2 * time.Second
+
+	// pluginCacheFileName sits beside versioncheck's version_check.json in
+	// the global config directory.
+	pluginCacheFileName = "plugin_version_check.json"
+)
+
+// pluginVersionCache is the plugin analog of versioncheck.VersionCache,
+// keyed by plugin name. No SkippedVersion: there is no interactive prompt,
+// so there is no "skip this version" choice to remember.
+type pluginVersionCache struct {
+	Plugins map[string]pluginVersionCheckState `json:"plugins"`
+}
+
+type pluginVersionCheckState struct {
+	LastCheckTime time.Time `json:"last_check_time"`
+}
+
+// listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck is a test seam over the tag resolution
+// `entire plugin upgrade` uses.
+var listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = listRemoteSemverTags
+
+// checkPluginUpdateAndNotify prints an update notice for pluginName when a
+// newer stable tag than the installed one exists. Silent on all errors to
+// avoid interrupting plugin runs, mirroring versioncheck.CheckAndNotify.
+//
+// Plugins without an install manifest (local-dev symlinks, binaries dropped
+// on PATH) and pinned installs are skipped — the same installs
+// `entire plugin upgrade` skips.
+func checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(ctx context.Context, w io.Writer, pluginName string) {
+	m, err := LoadPluginManifest(pluginName)
+	if err != nil || m == nil {
+		return
+	}
+	if m.Pinned {
+		return
+	}
+
+	cache := loadPluginVersionCache()
+	if time.Since(cache.Plugins[pluginName].LastCheckTime) < pluginCheckInterval {
+		return
+	}
+
+	tagCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, pluginCheckTimeout)
+	tags, err := listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck(tagCtx, m.RepoURL)
+	cancel()
+
+	// Always stamp the cache so a failing remote is not retried on every
+	// invocation.
+	cache.Plugins[pluginName] = pluginVersionCheckState{LastCheckTime: time.Now()}
+	if saveErr := savePluginVersionCache(cache); saveErr != nil {
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "plugin version check: failed to save cache",
+			"plugin", pluginName, "error", saveErr.Error())
+	}
+
+	if err != nil {
+		logging.Debug(ctx, "plugin version check: failed to list tags",
+			"plugin", pluginName, "error", err.Error())
+		return
+	}
+	if len(tags) == 0 {
+		return
+	}
+
+	// Same comparison UpgradeInstalledPlugin makes before reinstalling.
+	latest := tags[0]
+	if semver.Compare(canonicalSemver(latest), canonicalSemver(m.Tag)) <= 0 {
+		return
+	}
+
+	fmt.Fprintf(w, "\nPlugin update available! %s %s -> %s\nTo update, run:\n  entire plugin upgrade %s\n",
+		pluginName, strings.TrimPrefix(m.Tag, "v"), strings.TrimPrefix(latest, "v"), pluginName)
+}
+
+// loadPluginVersionCache returns the cached per-plugin check times, or an
+// empty cache when the file is missing or unreadable — mirroring how
+// versioncheck treats its cache file.
+func loadPluginVersionCache() *pluginVersionCache {
+	empty := &pluginVersionCache{Plugins: map[string]pluginVersionCheckState{}}
+	root, err := userdirs.ConfigRootForRead()
+	if err != nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	data, err := osroot.ReadFileNoFollow(root, pluginCacheFileName)
+	if err != nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	var cache pluginVersionCache
+	if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &cache); err != nil || cache.Plugins == nil {
+		return empty
+	}
+	return &cache
+}
+
+// savePluginVersionCache writes the cache with the same atomic
+// write-then-rename versioncheck's saveCache uses. Going through
+// userdirs.ConfigRoot also creates the config directory with private
+// permissions when this runs before first login.
+func savePluginVersionCache(cache *pluginVersionCache) error {
+	data, err := json.MarshalIndent(cache, "", "  ")
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("marshaling cache: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	root, err := userdirs.ConfigRoot()
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("opening config directory: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	tmpFile, tmpName, err := jsonutil.CreateTempIn(root, pluginCacheFileName)
+	if err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("creating temp file: %w", err)
+	}
+	defer func() { _ = root.Remove(tmpName) }() //nolint:errcheck // best-effort; a successful rename already consumed it
+
+	if _, err := tmpFile.Write(data); err != nil {
+		_ = tmpFile.Close() // cleanup on error path
+		return fmt.Errorf("writing cache: %w", err)
+	}
+	if err := tmpFile.Close(); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("closing temp file: %w", err)
+	}
+
+	if err := root.Rename(tmpName, pluginCacheFileName); err != nil {
+		return fmt.Errorf("renaming cache file: %w", err)
+	}
+	return nil
+}

+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"errors"
+	"strings"
+	"testing"
+	"time"
+
+	"github.com/entireio/cli/internal/entireclient/userdirs"
+)
+
+// setupPluginUpdateCheck isolates the managed plugin dir and the global
+// config dir (where the check's cache lives), installs a manifest for
+// "brain" at v0.1.0, and stubs the remote tag listing.
+func setupPluginUpdateCheck(t *testing.T, manifest *PluginManifest, tags []string, tagsErr error) *int {
+	t.Helper()
+	withPluginDir(t)
+	t.Setenv(userdirs.EnvConfigDir, t.TempDir())
+	if manifest != nil {
+		if err := SavePluginManifest(manifest); err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("SavePluginManifest: %v", err)
+		}
+	}
+	calls := 0
+	orig := listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck
+	listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = func(context.Context, string) ([]string, error) {
+		calls++
+		return tags, tagsErr
+	}
+	t.Cleanup(func() { listPluginTagsForUpdateCheck = orig })
+	return &calls
+}
+
+func brainManifest() *PluginManifest {
+	return &PluginManifest{Name: "brain", RepoURL: "https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain", Tag: "v0.1.0"}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_NotifiesWhenOutdated(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"v0.2.0", "v0.1.0"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1", *calls)
+	}
+	got := out.String()
+	for _, want := range []string{"Plugin update available! brain 0.1.0 -> 0.2.0", "entire plugin upgrade brain"} {
+		if !strings.Contains(got, want) {
+			t.Errorf("notice %q missing %q", got, want)
+		}
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SilentWhenUpToDate(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	// "0.1.0" vs installed "v0.1.0": equal under semver, so no notice —
+	// same spelling tolerance UpgradeInstalledPlugin has.
+	setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"0.1.0"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output, got %q", out.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_CacheSuppressesRecheck(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), []string{"v0.2.0"}, nil)
+
+	var first, second strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &first, "brain")
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &second, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1 (second call must hit the 24h cache)", *calls)
+	}
+	if second.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output on cached call, got %q", second.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_FetchFailureIsSilentAndStampsCache(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, brainManifest(), nil, errors.New("network down"))
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("expected no output, got %q", out.String())
+	}
+	if *calls != 1 {
+		t.Fatalf("tag listings = %d, want 1 (a failed check must not retry within 24h)", *calls)
+	}
+	state := loadPluginVersionCache().Plugins["brain"]
+	if time.Since(state.LastCheckTime) > time.Minute {
+		t.Fatalf("cache not stamped after failed fetch: %v", state.LastCheckTime)
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SkipsPinned(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	m := brainManifest()
+	m.Pinned = true
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, m, []string{"v9.9.9"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 0 || out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("pinned plugin checked remote (%d calls) or printed %q", *calls, out.String())
+	}
+}
+
+func TestPluginUpdateCheck_SkipsWithoutManifest(t *testing.T) { //nolint:paralleltest // mutates env
+	calls := setupPluginUpdateCheck(t, nil, []string{"v9.9.9"}, nil)
+
+	var out strings.Builder
+	checkPluginUpdateAndNotify(t.Context(), &out, "brain")
+
+	if *calls != 0 || out.Len() != 0 {
+		t.Fatalf("manifest-less plugin checked remote (%d calls) or printed %q", *calls, out.String())
+	}
+}

if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

<result>The per-run file reads are not where the cost is. Both files are tiny, and reading them costs microseconds, far less than starting the plugin process. The real problems are on the path that runs once a day, and three of them can stall or repeat the `git ls-remote`. Ranked by impact:

**1. The 2s timeout does not actually cap the stall** (`cmd/entire/cli/plugin_versioncheck.go:76`, through `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_gitremote.go:119-137`)
- **Summary:** When the 2s deadline hits, Go kills only the `git` process. `runGitQuiet` sends stdout and stderr to custom writers (`limitedWriter`), so Go copies them through pipes, and it sets no `cmd.WaitDelay`. Git's child processes (`git-remote-https`, or `ssh` for ssh remotes) inherit the stderr pipe. `cmd.Run()` waits for those pipes to close, which only happens when the orphaned children exit on their own network timeouts. So the "at most 2s" pause after a plugin run can last much longer. That bug already existed for interactive installs, but this change puts it on a path that hooks and agents hit constantly.
- **Cheaper alternative:** set `cmd.WaitDelay` (for example 100–250ms) in `runGitQuiet`, or put git in its own process group and kill the whole group when the deadline hits.

**2. A failed cache save means `git ls-remote` runs on every invocation** (`plugin_versioncheck.go:75-85`, `:136`)
- **Summary:** The network call happens first, and only then is the cache stamped. If the config directory can't be written (sandboxed agents, read-only `$HOME`, containers), `savePluginVersionCache` fails, the failure is only logged at debug level, and every later `entire brain`/`graph` run pays the full ls-remote again. The CLI's own `versioncheck.CheckAndNotify` avoids this by returning early when `ensureGlobalConfigDir` fails, before it touches the network.
- **Cheaper alternative:** open `userdirs.ConfigRoot()` (or write the stamp) before the network call, and return without the ls-remote if that fails.

**3. Parallel runs all fire `git ls-remote` at once** (`plugin_versioncheck.go:70-82`)
- **Summary:** The stamp is written only after the ls-remote finishes, up to 2s or more later. Agents often run several `entire brain`/`graph` calls in parallel or in quick succession from hooks. Every run that starts while the stale check is in flight passes the gate and starts its own ls-remote.
- **Cheaper alternative:** write `LastCheckTime = now` right after the gate passes and before the network call. It's a cheap claim: there is a small race window, but no N-way fan-out.

**4. The two post-run checks run one after the other** (`cmd/entire/cli/plugin.go:180-182`)
- **Summary:** `postPluginVersionCheck` (2s HTTP budget) and then `postPluginUpdateCheck` (2s git budget, more given finding 1) run in sequence. On a run where both are stale, such as the first run of the day, the user waits up to about 4s+ after the plugin has already exited.
- **Cheaper alternative:** run both checks in goroutines that each write to a buffer, wait for both, then print the buffers in a fixed order. The worst case becomes max(a, b) instead of a + b. Notices still never interleave.

**5. Minor: the manifest is read and parsed before the cheaper 24h gate** (`plugin_versioncheck.go:62` vs `:70-71`)
- **Summary:** On almost every run the 24h gate is what returns early. The current order still opens the plugin root, reads `manifest.yml` and runs a reflection-based YAML parse before reading the JSON cache. The cost is tiny (tens of microseconds), so this is tidiness, not a real hot-path cost.
- **Cheaper alternative:** load the cache and check `time.Since(...)` first, then call `LoadPluginManifest` only once the cache is stale. The two reads aren't otherwise linked; the pinned and no-manifest checks still work after the reorder.

These look fine:
- Both directory handles come from the shared cached handle (`osroot.Shared`), so nothing is reopened per call.
- The cache file is one JSON map that grows by one small entry per installed plugin. Pruning it isn't worth doing.
- There are no long-lived closures; the deferred cleanup closure in `savePluginVersionCache` is short and holds only `root` and `tmpName`.

I made no edits.</result>

On deadline Go kills `git`, but `git-remote-https`/`ssh` children inherit the pipe write-ends and survive, so `Run` blocks until they exit on their own network timeouts. The stall was pre-existing but sat on interactive install commands; this PR puts it on the post-run path agents hit constantly. Fix at the root: set `cmd.WaitDelay` (~1s) in `runGitQuiet` — one line, covers all callers. *(Verified in source.)*

**[important] `plugin_versioncheck.go:70-85` — the mirror missed versioncheck's pre-network gate, and the stamp lands too late**
`CheckAndNotify` returns early via `ensureGlobalConfigDir` *before* touching the network; my version fetches first and stamps after. Two consequences: with an unwritable config dir (sandboxed agent, read-only HOME) the debug-logged save failure means **every** plugin run pays the ls-remote; and concurrent runs that pass the gate while a check is in flight each start their own ls-remote. Since the cache stores only `LastCheckTime`, stamping **before** the fetch fixes both at once: a failed write returns before the network, and parallel runs see the claim.

**[important] `global_test.go` / `plugin_store.go:66` — plugin-dir test isolation is missing at the root, and this PR widens the exposure**
`TestMain` isolates `ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR` but not the plugin dir, and `userdirs` has a `testdirs` fallback for config that `pluginParentDir` lacks (a gap `plugin_on_demand_test.go` already notes). The new unintercepted call means the five `MaybeRunPlugin` success-path tests now load the developer's **real** plugin manifests — a matching name triggers a real `git ls-remote` and a stray banner mid-test (CI unaffected; dev machines flaky). Fix once, not per test: add a `testdirs.Dir("plugins")` fallback in `pluginParentDir` and set `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR` in `TestMain`, matching the config-dir pattern.

**[important] `plugin.go:107,182` — the new seam is never stubbed or asserted**
Nothing tests that `postPluginUpdateCheck` fires on exit 0 (parity with `TestMaybeRunPlugin_VersionCheckAfterSuccess`), and `interceptVersionCheck` swaps only the CLI notice, so `*VersionCheck*` tests run half the post-run behavior for real. Either merge both notices into one seam (`postPluginRunNotices`, holding the self-update guard internally) so the existing intercept covers both, or keep two seams, have the helper swap both, and add a wiring assertion. One agent suggested deleting the seam as unused — rejected: the stub is exactly what the tests above need.

**[important] `plugin_versioncheck.go:130-159` — hand-rolled atomic write duplicates `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn`** *(unanimous, 4/4 agents)*
~20 copied lines (from versioncheck's pre-helper-era `saveCache`) collapse to `jsonutil.WriteFileAtomicIn(root, pluginCacheFileName, data, 0o600)` — identical semantics plus symlink-safe parent pinning; precedent at `agent/agent_homes.go:65`.

**[nit] `plugin_versioncheck.go:61-101` — the newer-tag decision is copied from `UpgradeInstalledPlugin`, not shared**
The doc comment's promise that the notice "can never name a version the upgrade would not install" is enforced only by the copies staying in sync. Extracting one resolve helper both paths call would pin it.

**[nit] `plugin_versioncheck.go:42-48`** — the cache wrapper struct holds a map of one-field structs; `map[string]time.Time` does the same job.

**[nit] `plugin.go:180-182`** — on a both-stale day the two notices cost up to ~4s sequentially; parallelizing is possible but probably not worth the concurrency for a once-daily 2s.

**[nit] `plugin_versioncheck.go:62`** — the YAML manifest parse runs before the cheaper 24h cache gate; reversing the order trims the common path (microseconds — tidiness only).

Self-update guard correctly *not* applied to the plugin check (manifest is read fresh from disk); `agent-help` delegation calls `runPlugin` directly so the check doesn't fire there; notice is stderr-only (the old stdout-banner corruption class doesn't apply); package placement is right (`versioncheck` can't host it — import cycle, and sharing `version_check.json` would race two read-modify-write cycles).

### Summary
**Request changes** — the design and mirror are sound, docs and test coverage of the check function itself are good, but three things need fixing before merge: (1) stamp the cache before the network call (restores the missed mirror gate, kills the every-run-fetch and fan-out cases), (2) `cmd.WaitDelay` in `runGitQuiet` so the 2s budget actually binds, (3) plugin-dir test isolation + a wiring test for the new seam. To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

The key priority here is making sure the check never blocks or stalls normal CLI usage, which lines up with the WaitDelay fix and stamping before fetch. The user also mentions an alternative idea—auto-updating plugins when the CLI updates—but that's just a thought to note as a possible follow-up, not something to implement now.

From the review, I need to apply four fixes: stamp the cache before fetching to restore the config-dir gate semantics and prevent parallel fan-out; add `cmd.WaitDelay` to `runGitQuiet` so the 2s budget actually takes effect; fix test isolation with a `testdirs.Dir("plugins")` fallback and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR` in TestMain; and sort out the seam/test wiring question. I'm weighing whether to merge the two notice seams into one `postPluginRunNotices` function holding the guard, versus keeping both seams separate — merging simplifies things but risks losing the granularity that existing tests rely on to distinguish self-update behavior from normal version checks, so I'm leaning toward keeping both seams and extending the interceptor to stub and count both.

I'll refactor the interceptor into something like `interceptPluginNotices` that returns both a version-check counter and an update-check counter, update the existing tests to use it, and add new assertions confirming the update check fires on success and even after a self-update. I also need to check whether there's coverage for the nonzero-exit-code path, since notices should only run when the plugin exits cleanly.

For the write path, I'll swap in `WriteFileAtomic` for saving the plugin version cache. While I'm restructuring, it's cheap to flatten the cache to a simple map of strings to timestamps, reorder manifest parsing after the cache gate, and extract a shared helper with `UpgradeInstalledPlugin` so both paths mirror the same proven process without introducing new design.

On the refactor itself, I'm weighing whether extracting that shared helper is worth the churn since it touches the production upgrade path — given the instruction not to interfere with production, I'll skip it and note it as a follow-up in the PR. I'm also skipping the sequential 2s+2s batching idea since it adds complexity, and considering whether the whole check could be made fully non-blocking, though the synchronous nature of the version check makes that tricky without detaching the process.

With WaitDelay and a stamp-before-fetch approach, the worst case is still only about 2 seconds plus the wait delay once per 24 hours per plugin, matching the CLI's existing guarantee, so that's acceptable. My plan is to edit the version check file to reorder the logic: gate on cache first, then load the manifest, stamp and save, fetch, compare, and notify, flattening the cache type and using atomic file writes — I need to make sure manifest-less or pinned plugins return without stamping so no network call happens and they get re-evaluated next time.

The key behavioral change is that if saving the stamp fails, I log it and return before fetching at all, deliberately deviating from the normal post-fetch stamping to bound cost under an unwritable config directory, which I should document briefly in a comment. For the git command wrapper, I'm adding a WaitDelay of one second with a comment on pipe inheritance, and confirming that CommandContext's default cancellation behavior is to kill the process.

Checking whether the WaitDelay affects existing callers — it only kicks in after the context's own 2-minute timeout expires, so there's no real risk since waiting past that point was never useful anyway. For pluginParentDir, I'm looking at adding a testdirs fallback, referencing the configDir pattern that uses testdirs.Dir at userdirs.go:116, and confirming cli can import internal/testdirs. Then I need to check what ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR setup is needed in global_test.go's TestMain.

Beyond that, I should extend the intercept helper in plugin_test.go with a new wiring test, update plugin_versioncheck_test.go for the flattened cache structure, and add a test where the config directory is unwritable — pointing ENTIRE_CONFIG_DIR at a file path so ConfigRoot fails, which should prevent any fetch from happening.

I also need to double-check that the existing FetchFailureIsSilentAndStampsCache test still holds since stamping now happens before fetching, and update the external-commands.md docs to reflect the stamp-before-fetch behavior.

For running checks, I'll do fmt, lint, unit tests, and integration tests locally, but skip canary since it fails in this environment and is covered by CI instead — I'll note that in my response. content.thinking:
With the patterns settled, I'm adding a fallback to plugin_store.go that checks testdirs for a plugins directory, placing it right after the environment override branch so it mirrors the same ordering used for configDir.

Now I'm restructuring plugin_versioncheck.go: introducing a pluginVersionCache type tracking last-check time per plugin name (no skip-version concept since there's no interactive prompt), and rewriting checkPluginUpdateAndNotify to load the cache, bail early if the interval hasn't elapsed, load the manifest, skip pinned plugins, and stamp the cache before the network call rather than after.

The stamping-before logic exists because an unwritable config dir needs to cost zero network calls and plugin runs arrive concurrently from agent hooks, so claiming the slot early prevents multiple parallel ls-remote calls. If the cache save fails or tag listing errors out or returns nothing, the function just logs and returns.

Now I'm writing the cache load and save helpers: loading reads the config root, tries to read the cache file, and unmarshals JSON, falling back to an empty cache on any error; saving marshals the cache back to indented JSON.

Wrapping the write error with context seems like the right approach, matching the pattern used elsewhere. I also realize the old file format with a different structure would just fail to unmarshal into the new map type, which is harmless since that format was never actually shipped.

{"id":"ENT-3598","uuid":"20b00a2f-9e11-4b23-9498-1dc31203bcda","title":"CLI: update notice for outdated plugins, mirroring the CLI's own version check","description":"## Problem

The CLI notifies the user when the `entire` binary is outdated: a version check runs after commands, caches its result for 24 hours, and prints "Update available! x -> y" to stderr (`versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`). Installed plugins have no equivalent. A user on an old plugin version sees nothing until they manually run `entire plugin upgrade`.

## Approach

Reuse the proven mechanisms; no new design.

* **Trigger**: after a successful plugin run, next to the existing CLI version notice in the plugin dispatch path (`plugin.go`). Check only the plugin that ran.
* **Latest version**: `listRemoteSemverTags` on the manifest's repo URL — the same resolution `entire plugin upgrade` uses (stable semver tags only, prereleases excluded).
* **Cadence**: 24-hour per-plugin cache in the global config dir, beside `version_check.json`. The cache updates even when the fetch fails, so a network problem does not retry on every invocation. Silent on all errors. All mirrored from `versioncheck.CheckAndNotify`.
* **Notice** (stderr, mirrors the CLI banner's non-interactive form):

  ```
  Plugin update available! brain 0.2.0 -> 0.3.0
  To update, run:
    entire plugin upgrade brain
  ```
* **Skipped**: plugins without an install manifest (local-dev symlinks, binaries dropped on PATH) and pinned installs — the same installs `plugin upgrade` skips.

## Non-goals

* Interactive auto-upgrade prompt (parity with `maybeAutoUpdate`). Plugin runs are mostly agent-driven and non-interactive; the printed command is the useful part. Can follow up if wanted.
* Checking plugins other than the one being run.
* New kill-switch env vars.

## Follow-up idea (not in scope)
